주제찾기
1 1번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
In Korea, showing respect is not merely good manners; it is built into the grammar itself. An exchange student found that choosing the right level of politeness demanded constant attention. At her home-stay family's table she answered her host father with a casual word instead of a polite one. Only later did she learn that the situation had called for the respectful form. In a lecture hall she asked her professor to explain again, but used the pronoun reserved for close friends. Every head in the room turned toward her, and she froze without knowing why. The professor, however, recognized that she was still learning and let the moment pass. She remains puzzled by honorific words, yet expects that practice and advice will eventually make them natural.
①the trouble a learner faces in handling Korea's language of respect
②the reasons Korean grammar has become simpler over recent decades
③the advantages of studying abroad while living with a host family
④the strategies professors use to correct students during lectures
⑤the difficulty of translating polite expressions into English
2 2번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
A visitor praises Seoul's subway for being clean, punctual, and impressive in nearly every respect. Over ten lines run through the capital, and trains reach the next station in only a minute or three. Every car is cooled in summer, and in winter the seats themselves are warmed. Riders connect to the internet for free, and switching between a bus and a train costs less than paying twice. Certain seats are held for expectant mothers, elderly riders, and passengers with disabilities. Those seats, the writer argues, reveal a habit of thinking about people who need help. A Norwegian reader adds that a short bus ride at home costs far more than a subway trip in Seoul. A Parisian reader notes that his own city ranks who may claim its priority seats first.
①the convenience of Seoul's subway and the culture of consideration behind it
②the engineering that allows trains to arrive within three minutes
③the financial burden that low fares place on public transport systems
④the legal rules that decide who may sit in a reserved seat
⑤the reasons why foreign visitors prefer buses to subways

주제찾기
3 3번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
Eating out in Korea impresses visitors from the very first order. Ask for one dish from the menu and a row of small side dishes arrives with it, all at no cost. Diners who finish those little plates may simply request more of them. The food itself usually reaches the table within ten minutes of ordering. Delivery works the same way, moving at what one writer calls lightning speed. Nearly any meal can be ordered and left waiting at a doorstep almost immediately. The same hurry shows up outside restaurants, as audiences leave theaters before the closing credits begin. Speed, it seems, has become a shared habit rather than a restaurant policy.
①generosity and speed as twin marks of Korean dining culture
②the economic reasons why Korean restaurants keep prices low
③the difficulty foreigners face when reading a Korean menu
④the growing demand for slow food among young Koreans
⑤how delivery apps changed the schedules of Korean workers
4 4번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
A few habits are worth learning before you spend time in Korean homes and buildings. The first is simple: leave your shoes at the door of anyone's house. Never write a person's name in red, since that color calls to mind death and misfortune. Never leave a spoon or chopsticks standing upright in a bowl of rice either. That arrangement belongs to meals prepared for someone who has died. In many buildings the fourth-floor button is marked with an F instead of a number. The reason is that four is pronounced almost like the word meaning death. Elsewhere the rules differ: in parts of Brazil a thumb-and-finger ring is read as an insult.
①everyday taboos in Korea and the beliefs that lie behind them
②the historical origin of Korean funeral ceremonies for ancestors
③practical advice on renting an apartment in a Korean city
④how hand gestures developed differently in Asia and Latin America
⑤the difficulty of pronouncing Korean numbers correctly

5 1번 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
Respect runs so deep in Korean culture that the language encodes it in every sentence ending. A newly arrived student discovered how many choices that single fact forces on a speaker. Answering her host father, she used the informal word rather than the respectful one. The embarrassment came afterward, when someone explained which form she should have chosen. A second slip followed in class, where she addressed her professor with an informal pronoun. The whole room turned to look, and panic set in before she understood her mistake. Her professor read the situation kindly and let her continue without comment. Confusion has not disappeared, but she is confident that steady practice will settle it.

A meal in a Korean restaurant begins with more food than you actually ordered. Small side dishes are set down beside the main dish without any extra charge. If a plate runs empty, you may ask the staff to fill it again. Visitors read this habit as a sign of how openhanded their hosts are. What surprises them next is how quickly the kitchen works. Most orders are cooked and served in under ten minutes. Delivery riders bring almost any dish to a doorstep in scarcely more time. Even in movie theaters, people are already standing up as the credits begin.

8 4번 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
Travelers who want to avoid awkward moments in Korea should learn a handful of rules. Shoes come off at the doorway of any private home. A name written in red is unwelcome, because red carries associations with death and misfortune. A spoon standing straight up in rice is unwelcome for the same reason. Koreans arrange rice that way only when the meal is offered to someone who has died. Even elevator panels show the belief, replacing the fourth-floor number with the letter F. Four is avoided because it sounds close to the word meaning death. Each rule looks small, yet breaking one can offend a host far more than a visitor expects.
①사소해 보이는 금기에도 죽음에 관한 믿음이 담겨 있으므로 미리 알아 두어야 한다.
②한국의 주거 문화는 다른 나라보다 위생을 훨씬 중요하게 여긴다.
③외국인은 한국어 숫자를 정확히 발음하는 법부터 배워야 한다.
④문화적 차이는 결국 시간이 지나면 저절로 사라지게 마련이다.
⑤손님을 맞이하는 예절은 나라마다 법으로 규정되어 있다.

12 4번 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
Some rules in Korea are easy to break by accident and awkward to explain afterward. Shoes stay outside the living space, left neatly at the entrance of a home. Red ink is kept away from names, because the color suggests death and ill fortune. Upright chopsticks in rice are avoided, since that setting is meant for the dead. Buildings often label the fourth floor F rather than print the number itself. The number four is shunned because its sound resembles the word for death. A visitor who learns these few points will rarely offend anyone by mistake. The same caution travels well: a friendly gesture at home may insult someone abroad.

27 3번 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
In a Korean restaurant one order brings a tray of side dishes that cost nothing. Guests may ask for more of them as often as they like. The main dish itself is usually cooked and served in under ten minutes. Delivery riders bring almost any meal to a doorstep almost as fast. Outside restaurants the same rhythm appears, as audiences leave before the credits end. A Tagalog speaker even reports a word, "dali-dali," that sounds and means much like "ppalli-ppalli." Taken together, these scenes suggest that . The hurry is not a rule of the kitchen but a habit of everyday life.
①haste has spread far beyond the dinner table into daily life
②restaurants deliberately train their customers to eat quickly
③generosity and speed cannot exist in the same food culture
④foreign visitors rarely notice how fast Koreans finish a meal
⑤language differences make cultural comparison almost impossible
28 4번 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
Several small rules protect a visitor from embarrassing moments in Korea. Shoes come off at the door, and a name is never written in red ink. A spoon or chopsticks left standing in rice is avoided as well. Rice is served that way only for someone who has died. In elevators the fourth-floor button often shows an F rather than a number. Four is pronounced almost like the word meaning death. Taken together, these customs show that Koreans . A guest who understands that will read each rule at a glance.
①avoid anything that recalls death in daily life
②prefer foreign designs to traditional building styles
③regard silence as the highest form of politeness
④value speed more than accuracy in everyday work
⑤consider red the most fortunate color of all

서술형 (본문 제시) · 1번
Respect is a big thing in Korean culture, and it shows even in their language. Korean honorifics are very confusing. There are simply so many things to consider. My first embarrassing moment took place when my home-stay dad asked me to tell his wife to come for dinner. I responded, "응 (Okay)," to his request. I was embarrassed to learn that I should have said, "네," in that situation. Another uncomfortable situation occurred in a classroom. When I didn't hear the professor clearly, I said, "교수님, 이해가 안 되요. '너'가 다시 설명해 주세요. (Professor, I didn't catch what you said. Could you repeat it?)" The moment I uttered it, everyone turned around and looked at me. I thought, "Why is everybody staring at me? Did I do anything wrong?" I panicked. Luckily, the professor understood my situation. I'm still confused about honorific words, but with practice and guidance, I'm sure I will get the hang of it. It was also interesting that words like "언니," "누나," "형," and "오빠" are not just for brothers and sisters in Korea. For example, "누나 (older sister)" is commonly used to address an older female friend even though she is not your own sister by blood. Speaking of "오빠," I was confused when I first heard "oppa" because it is pronounced almost the same as "opa" in German, which means "grandpa." It was also funny that "엄마" meaning "mom" also sounds like "oma," the German word for grandma.

Seoul's subway is terrific in terms of cleanliness, reliability, and almost every other aspect imaginable. It has more than ten lines with an estimated time of mostly 1 to 3 minutes between subway stops, allowing you to easily get around the city and its suburbs. It is fully air-conditioned. It even has heated seats in the winter. The free Wi-Fi on the subway is also a nice touch. Plus, there are transfer discounts between buses and subways. The subway even has specially reserved seats for pregnant women as well as for seniors and people with disabilities. The subway reflects the national character of being considerate to others, especially those in need. Easy to use and super cheap compared to other countries! Here in a town without subway, a one-way bus ticket to town (3 km) costs about 7,000 won. So to a Norwegian, the subway in Seoul is way cheap! The Paris Metro also has "priority seats" which should be reserved for those who need them most. However, there is a kind of ranking system. Disabled war veterans get the highest priority. Then in order come the visually-challenged, mobility-impaired, pregnant women, people with toddlers, and then finally seniors over 75.
